so_what: 21% of all pings come from ships sitting still at anchorage and 57% from berths: the zones capture real port behaviour.
Ships funnel through two approach lanes; anchorage pressure builds just outside them, so approach scheduling is where coordination pays off.
Hotspot A and Hotspot B alone hold 29% of all anchor ship-hours: monitor these two spots first.
The queue ranges from 2 to 12 ships and sits in High (>8) for 21% of hours: congestion is recurring, not a one-off.

visual: Time from port entry to berth
so_what: 105 of 123 ships reach berth in about 3.5 h; 18 wait a median of 23 h (up to 114 h). Those 18 ships cause 95% of all delay hours.
36% of tankers are delayed vs 10% of cargo ships (Fisher p = 0.004): tanker berth requests need earlier confirmation.
36% of arrivals come between 00:00 and 04:00 local time: roster pilots and tugs for that window.
Queue size does not depend on time of day (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.36): a fixed daily timetable will not fix congestion.

Rougher sea went with SHORTER queues (rho -0.34, -0.30 after removing the trend), and ships at berth rise as the queue drains (rho -0.47): the opposite of 'bad weather causes delays'. With 2 weeks of data this is association only; weather added little to forecasts.
The daily average queue swings from 3.4 to 10.3 ships: plan buffers by the day, not by the hour.
At the middle assumed rate ($30,000/ship/day) the queue cost about $2.0M in 11 days; cutting it 10% avoids about $0.20M. Rates are assumptions.
At 3 h the naive rule wins (error 0.79 vs 1.02); at 24 h the model cuts error by 32% (3.01 to 2.04 ships). Use the model for day-ahead planning.
Forecasts made a day ahead follow the swings but miss sharp peaks (RMSE 2.5 ships): treat them as a planning signal, not a promise.
Logistic Regression classifier catches 19 of 32 High hours with 8 false alarms; the naive rule catches 15 with 33 false alarms.
